title: Mycenaean Greece
capsule: Mycenaean Greece was the dominant Bronze Age civilization of the Greek mainland (c. 1600–1100 BCE), named for the citadel of Mycenae in the Argolid from which its most characteristic palace complexes, shaft graves, and Linear B administrative tablets have been excavated. Under a wanax (king), palace centers at Mycenae, Tiryns, Pylos, Thebes, and elsewhere controlled redistributive economies, organized military expeditions — the legendary Trojan War finds its historical analogue in this period — and traded widely across the Mediterranean. The civilization collapsed abruptly around 1200–1100 BCE in a cascade involving destroyed palaces, disrupted trade, and population movements, contributing to the broader Bronze Age collapse; Linear B writing disappeared and Greece entered a 'Dark Age' of reduced complexity for some 400 years.
attestation: Boundaries from Seshat Cliopatria (Bennett et al., Scientific Data 2025; CC BY 4.0), digitized from standard historical atlases at ~0.07° resolution. Palace sites are archaeologically well identified; the territorial reach of each palatial center and whether a single Mycenaean state or a system of competing polities existed are actively debated among scholars.
